Record cards expose source-native values under their original column names.

to measured absolute or relative bioavailability and matched oral-versus-

sampling context together.

L2 adds related experimental records for the same molecule and exact condition.

formulation, dose, study design, consistency, limitations, or why an L1 outcome

oral-bioavailability outcome.

records did not define the accepted gold outcome: never count them as extra gold
votes, and do not treat the L1/L2 name itself as a positive or negative label.

parent-condition context may apply to the query. It is not a positive-class
probability, an experimental result, or a substitute for reasoning about the
visible structure, endpoint, assay, species, formulation, exposure, and
condition. Infer direction from the record cards first, then judge transfer from
all visible context. Do not invent a numeric similarity judgment or assume that
a higher transfer_likelihood must outweigh a concrete experimental mismatch.

Use general medicinal-chemistry knowledge to interpret structures, but ground
every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited
record cards. Repeated records and multiple cards from one context are not
independent evidence. Return exactly one valid JSON object and do not reveal
hidden chain-of-thought.

claims.claim: Query is chlorothiazide, the unsaturated benzothiadiazine analog of hydrochlorothiazide (M01 in L3); L3 records show oral HCTZ produces dose-dependent systemic exposure in humans (Cmax ~61–197 ng/mL at 12.5–25 mg; AUC0-24 ~398–1109 ng·h/mL), indicating meaningful oral absorption for the closest structural analog.

Visible L1 gold records for sulfonamide/related contexts report human F values ≥30% (valdecoxib ~83%, fasudil 69%, sildenafil 41%); the only sub-20% record (C31) is rat fasudil and is species-specific, not transferable.

L6 hepatic clearance/metabolic-stability records show low hepatic extraction or scarce metabolism for related sulfonamide diuretics (bumetanide negligible hepatic extraction C72; furosemide scarcely metabolized in human hepatocytes C81; azosemide low rat microsomal CLint C75/C74 and low M1 formation CLint C76) and low intrinsic clearance/no oxidative metabolism for lorazepam/oxazepam (C73/C77/C82/C83), supporting that hepatic first-pass loss is unlikely to drive F below 20% for a related sulfonamide diuretic.

L4 permeability and L5 gut-wall efflux/intestinal-metabolism records are for other molecules (celecoxib, tamsulosin, compound 2c, indapamide, PF-06282999, M11, trantinterol, compound 7l, compounds 82/87) and are formulation-, species-, or compound-specific; they do not affirmatively establish F<20% for chlorothiazide.

No direct absolute oral bioavailability or intestinal absorption measurement for chlorothiazide is present; the unfavorable passive-permeability prior (low logD, high TPSA, partial ionization) is insufficient to override the HCTZ exposure, L1 sulfonamide F values, and L6 low-clearance context.

evidence_gaps: No direct absolute oral bioavailability measurement for chlorothiazide in visible records.
No direct intestinal absorption, permeability, efflux, or hepatic clearance assay for chlorothiazide; L4/L5/L6 records are for other molecules.
L3 HCTZ Cmax/AUC records lack IV comparison, so fraction absorbed and first-pass extraction cannot be quantified directly.

Transfer from hydrochlorothiazide and other sulfonamide diuretics is structural/class-based, not identity; chlorothiazide's unsaturated benzothiadiazine and low logD may reduce absorption relative to HCTZ, but no affirmative evidence it falls below 20%.
No human metabolism/clearance data for chlorothiazide; first-pass extraction is unknown, though L6 related records suggest low hepatic clearance.
